doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Reissues, late audit payment and lawyers running labels
summary: Reissues earned labels money; Purdie got paid in 1994 for 1972 Prestige records after demanding an audit, and criticizes lawyers running companies.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Jazz reissues and all those kinds of things.

Everything. The jazz reissues they made gobbles of money. They didn’t have to pay anybody. So people like myself who also made records in the sixties and the seventies, my records, took off. Took off. Columbia, Prestige, Flying Dutchman. Those labels are owned by the big guys and they are making money with them. I finally got paid, twenty years later, twenty years later, from 1972, the record that I made on Prestige. 1972. ’71 and ’72. They started paying me in ’94 because I was smart enough to go in and say I want an audit.

Then all of a sudden, bam, the $4,445 they said I owed them for twenty years got paid. Now in the eighties — they were making money on my records in the late eighties. Millions. I find this out. I don’t get it. But they started making money and it was like what is happening? Of course you see revival — people were calling me from Europe

and they wanted my old records. They wanted my albums. I said my albums? I said, “But I’m making CDs.” “No, no, we want your albums.” That’s when I find out. And I’m selling. All my old stuff is selling. So I started to watch the industry a lot more. And a lot closer. As I was going along I saw what was happening and I saw how the big guys basically just kept getting bigger and bigger and bigger until the bubble started to burst and it was bursting because the people that they have running the companies were not musical people. They were lawyers. Lawyers were running the companies by the numbers, the books. How many units did we sell? What did we sell? It’s all about selling. It’s not about the quality. It’s all about the quantity to them. How much is the bottom line? We don’t have to pay for this do we? We got this. And that’s what they did. So they flourished for a lot of years. That last ten years, man serious trouble. Because they have nothing new. And everything they have new has gone by the wayside. They’re not selling millions. They might sell a hundred thousand, two hundred thousand, half a million units. But the money that they’ve already spent is not covering. Because you’ve got so many other people that are coming in and other little companies that are siphoning from them from the bottom. Because they’re not up there in their ivory towers, they’re down here and folks like me who are actually surviving and having a nice survival are actually earning a good living. Decent and good. You don’t have to sell a hundred thousand units to make ten or twenty thousand dollars. And you have to ask yourself, what do you mean, how come you don’t — because you can sell ten thousand units and make twenty thousand dollars. What? What? What are you talking about? Yeah.
